label: Savoy Records
rationale: Savoy MG 12020 (1955) is the canonical LP gathering of Dizzy Gillespie's revolutionary 1945-46 bebop masters: thirteen 78-rpm sides from seven New York sessions, spanning the Parker-Gillespie small groups ('Groovin' High', 'Dizzy Atmosphere', 'All The Things You Are', 'Hot House', 'Salt Peanuts'), the Dexter Gordon sextet's 'Blue 'n' Boogie' (1945-02-09), the 1946 Sonny Stitt-Milt Jackson combos ('Oop Bop Sh' Bam', 'That's Earl Brother') and the 1946 big band ('Things To Come', 'One Bass Hit #2', 'Rays Idea', 'Our Delight', 'Emanon'). The Rough Guide to Jazz calls the album 'some of the key bebop small-group and big band recordings' (S2); Thomas Owens calls the title track 'the first famous bebop recording' and its contrafact of 'Whispering' 'the most complex jazz melody superimposed on a pre-existing chordal scheme' of its time (S10). The Encyclopedia of Popular Music rates the set 3/5 (S2); Scott Yanow, while calling the music classic, faults the package as 'so-so' for brevity and outdated liner notes (S2, quoting AllMusic). AllMusic styles the album Bop, Jazz Instrument and Trumpet Jazz (S1). These sides are founding documents of recorded bebop - the idiom's co-leader in small-group dialogue with Charlie Parker and in his own big-band writing - and this LP, with its Savoy Jazz CD descendants, is the standard vehicle through which they circulate. Year given as 1945 (first session year) per the candidate; the LP itself was released in 1955 (S1, S2, S4).

personnel_record.notes: Seven New York sessions over 1945-46, compiled by Savoy on the 1955 LP MG 12020; per S3 the masters originate in the Guild (1945) and Musicraft (1946) 78-rpm issues. Session-to-LP mapping (S3, matrix-linked): 1945-02-09 -> 'Blue 'n' Boogie' (G555, first issued Guild 1001); 1945-02-28 -> 'Groovin' High' (G554A-1), 'All The Things You Are' (G556) and 'Dizzy Atmosphere' (G557, unissued on 78 - first issued on this LP per S3); 1945-05-11 -> 'Salt Peanuts' (G565A-1) and 'Hot House' (G568A-1), first issued Guild 1003; 1946-05-15 -> 'Oop Bop Sha Bam' (5498) and 'That's Earl, Brother' (5500), first issued Musicraft 383; 1946-06-10 -> 'Our Delight' (5550, Musicraft 399); 1946-07-09 -> 'One Bass Hit Part 2' (5609, Musicraft 404), 'Ray's Idea' (5610, Musicraft 487) and 'Things To Come' (5611, Musicraft 447); 1946-11-12 -> 'Emanon' (5789, Musicraft 447). The 1945-02-09 sextet also recorded a take of 'Groovin' High' (G554) not used on the LP - the LP carries the 1945-02-28 take, the reworking the song literature calls the famous version (S10) - and the 1946-05-15 session's 'One Bass Hit Part 1' and 'A Handfulla Gimme' are not on the LP. 'One Bass Hit #2' is part two of the two-part Musicraft 404 78 ('Part 1' is not on the LP) - a part designation, not an alternate take. Conflicts preserved: Wikipedia's infobox 'Recorded 1945 - December 11, 1947' (S2) conflicts with S3 (latest session 1946-11-12) and S4 ('seven different sessions between February 1945 and November 1946'); a Discogs release note on r9339912 (S5) describing 'live sessions' conflicts with S3's studio matrices. Recording venues: S3 documents only 'NYC' for each session, and S9 likewise calls the 1945-02-28 site an 'unidentified recording studio, New York, NY' - no venue is named in any source consulted, so each session is recorded city-level with epistemic unk; the canonical-places list was not provided in this dispatch, so no site_slug is asserted and no complete site_new is possible. Production: no producer or engineer is credited for the 1945-46 sessions in any source consulted; S1 carries only reissue-era credits (Yujiro Kasai and Rudy Van Gelder, remastering); S5 documents Rudy Van Gelder as lacquer cut for the 1955 LP (runout matrices 'MG 12020A X20 1 C RVG') and Ozzie Cadena as the LP's liner-notes author - session engineering remains unk. Session vocalists not on LP tracks: Sarah Vaughan ('Lover Man', 1945-05-11), Alice Roberts and Gil Fuller (1946-05-15, on titles not on the LP) per S3; Gillespie is also credited 'vocal' on the 1945-05-11 and 1946-05-15 sessions (S3). Personnel conflicts preserved: S4's per-track credits diverge from S3's session mapping on several side-B musicians (Stitt, Jackson, Lewis, Dorham, Wright, Orr, Greenlea, Thomas, John Brown, Lucky, Leo Parker, Pee Wee Moore, Howard E. Johnson - detailed per entry); S1/S2 additionally omit Charles Greenlea, Pee Wee Moore and James Moody (all S3-documented on LP sessions) while including Lucky Thompson, whom S3 does not document on any LP session. Durations differ between S2 and S4/S7 (e.g. 'Hot House' 2:27 in S2 vs 3:13 in S4/S7; 'Rays Idea' 3:09 in S2 vs 2:24 in S4/S7) - transfer variations, not alternate takes; S4 durations used here. Apple's digital reissue (S7) keeps the 13 titles but reorders tracks 5-6 and 9-12 relative to the LP. S2 prints track titles slightly differently ('One Bass Hit, Pt. 2', 'Ray's Idea', 'That's Earl, Brother', 'Things to Come'); S4/S5 LP spellings are used, with 'Emanon' credited to Gillespie and 'Milton Shaw' (S1; S2 prints 'Shaw'). This is a compilation in the 78-era sense - thirteen roughly three-minute masters gathered onto one 12-inch LP - and documents the sessions, not a modern anthology across them.

ballot.case_for: These 1945–46 Guild and Musicraft masters are founding documents of recorded bebop, centered on the historic Gillespie-Parker small groups and extending into Gillespie's modern big-band writing. Thomas Owens calls "Groovin' High" the first famous bebop recording and highlights its unprecedented contrafact complexity (S10), while The Rough Guide to Jazz identifies the compilation as containing key bebop small-group and big-band recordings (S2). Its extraordinary personnel network—Parker, Dexter Gordon, Sonny Stitt, Milt Jackson, Kenny Clarke, Ray Brown, John Lewis, and others—gives it exceptional session gravity and enduring discovery value.
ballot.case_against: The 1955 Savoy LP is an archival compilation of thirteen short 78-rpm sides from seven sessions, not a unified album statement; its abrupt movement from Parker-Gillespie combos to later sextets and big-band charts can feel historically assembled rather than artistically sequenced. The dossier's critical-consensus evidence is narrower than ideal, relying chiefly on the Rough Guide and Owens, while Yanow reports a so-so package and the Encyclopedia of Popular Music rates it 3/5 (S2). Extensive conflicts between jazzdisco.org and Discogs over several 1946 personnel assignments further complicate the documentation, even though they do not undermine the music's importance.
ballot.recommendation: John should place this at the front of the must-have queue for a final inclusion decision, treating the compilation format and documentation issues as minor compared with its foundational bebop significance.
